stem: Production logs reveal that the agent misinterprets data from your MCP tools: Unix timestamps from get_customer, ISO 8601 dates from lookup_order, and numeric status codes (1=pending, 2=shipped). Some tools are third-party MCP servers you cannot modify. What's the most maintainable approach to normalize data formats?

options.A: Use a PostToolUse hook to intercept tool results and apply formatting transformations before agent processing
options.B: Add detailed format documentation to your system prompt explaining each tool's data conventions
options.C: Modify tools you control to return human-readable formats; create wrapper tools for third-party tools
options.D: Create a normalize_data tool that the agent calls after each data retrieval to transform values

correct_option_text: Use a PostToolUse hook to intercept tool results and apply formatting transformations before agent processing
explanation: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results before the agent processes them, making them the documented mechanism for normalizing heterogeneous formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) coming from different MCP servers, including third-party ones the team cannot modify.

B.text: Documenting tool conventions in the system prompt relies on the model interpreting raw heterogeneous data correctly each turn; that's exactly the failure mode the logs reveal, and prompts cannot reformat values.
B.citation_quote: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them

C.text: Wrapping tools you control plus building shadow wrappers for third-party servers is high-maintenance compared to a single PostToolUse hook that normalizes uniformly without per-tool engineering.
C.citation_quote: Implementing PostToolUse hooks to normalize heterogeneous data formats

D.text: A normalize_data tool the agent must remember to call adds an extra LLM-driven step that can be skipped or mis-applied; deterministic normalization belongs in a hook, not in optional model behavior.
D.citation_quote: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them

stem:
You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

After adding regional order backends, production traces show the agent sometimes misreads raw lookup_order payloads: one region returns status_code: 3, another returns state: "RETURN_PENDING", and a third includes nested timestamps. The agent's final responses are inconsistent, even though each backend response is technically valid. What change best improves reliability without modifying every MCP tool implementation?

options.A: Parse the assistant's final text for status words and retry lookup_order whenever inconsistent wording appears.
options.B: Expand the system prompt with every regional status mapping and ask Claude to normalize payloads during response generation.
options.C: Require each customer message to include the customer's region so Claude can choose the correct payload interpretation.
options.D: Add a PostToolUse hook that transforms lookup_order outputs into a canonical support-case structure before Claude receives them.

correct_option_text: Add a PostToolUse hook that transforms lookup_order outputs into a canonical support-case structure before Claude receives them.
explanation: A PostToolUse hook intercepts tool results after execution and transforms them before the model reasons over them (Task 1.5). Centralizing regional payload normalization in a hook standardizes heterogeneous status codes, state strings, and nested timestamps into a canonical structure without modifying any MCP tool implementation.

A.text: Parsing assistant text for status words and retrying on inconsistent wording is an anti-pattern; the guide warns against 'parsing natural language signals to determine loop termination' and similar text-parsing approaches.
A.citation_quote: Avoiding anti-patterns such as parsing natural language signals to determine loop termination

B.text: Expanding the system prompt with every regional status mapping asks Claude to normalize payloads probabilistically during text generation — an approach the guide contrasts unfavorably with deterministic hook-based transformation.
B.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

C.text: Requiring the customer to include their region is an unacceptable UX burden and doesn't actually normalize the payloads; it merely routes interpretation responsibility to Claude at generation time.
C.citation_quote: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them

stem:
You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Production logs show get_customer returns ISO 8601 timestamps and numeric loyalty tiers, while lookup_order returns Unix timestamps and numeric status codes. The agent sometimes miscomputes return windows or mislabels order status after otherwise successful tool calls. You cannot change upstream MCP servers this quarter, but you need consistent reasoning across cases. What change best addresses the reliability issue?

options.A: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts each tool result into canonical dates, status labels, and tier fields before Claude sees it.
options.B: Modify the final customer response parser to correct dates and statuses after Claude has already decided the resolution.
options.C: Route all cases with mixed timestamp formats directly to escalate_to_human until the upstream MCP servers are standardized.
options.D: Add system instructions telling Claude to remember each tool's timestamp format and translate status codes during every reasoning step.

correct_option_text: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts each tool result into canonical dates, status labels, and tier fields before Claude sees it.
explanation: The miscomputations happen after tool calls return successfully but before Claude reasons over the results. A PostToolUse hook is precisely designed to intercept tool results at that point and transform them before the model sees them—converting Unix timestamps to ISO 8601, decoding numeric status codes to human-readable labels, and normalizing loyalty tier representations. This gives Claude stable canonical inputs without requiring any changes to the upstream MCP servers.

B.text: Correcting dates and statuses in the final response parser happens after Claude has already reasoned about the data. Any incorrect resolution decisions (e.g., miscalculated return windows) made during reasoning cannot be undone by post-processing the output text.
B.citation_quote: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them

C.text: Routing all cases with mixed timestamp formats to human escalation abandons first-contact resolution for a large class of routine cases. The exam guide identifies escalation as appropriate for policy exceptions, not for tool data format differences that can be normalized programmatically.
C.citation_quote: Appropriate escalation triggers: customer requests for a human, policy exceptions/gaps (not just complex cases), and inability to make meaningful progress

D.text: System instructions asking Claude to remember each tool's format and translate codes during every reasoning step relies on probabilistic prompt compliance. The exam guide explicitly contrasts hooks (deterministic guarantees) with prompt instructions (probabilistic compliance) for this type of business rule.
D.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

stem: Your team's CLAUDE.md file has grown to over 500 lines, mixing TypeScript conventions, testing guidelines, API patterns, and deployment procedures. Developers find it difficult to locate and update relevant sections. What approach does Claude Code support for organizing project-level instructions into focused, topic-specific modules?

options.A: Split instructions into README.md files in relevant subdirectories, which Claude automatically loads as instructions
options.B: Define a .claude/config.yaml file that maps file patterns to specific sections within CLAUDE.md
options.C: Create separate markdown files in .claude/rules/, each covering one topic (e.g., testing.md, api-conventions.md)
options.D: Create multiple files named CLAUDE.md at different levels of the directory tree, each one overriding the parent's instructions

correct_option_text: Create separate markdown files in .claude/rules/, each covering one topic (e.g., testing.md, api-conventions.md)
explanation: Claude Code documents .claude/rules/ as the modular alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md. Each topic-specific markdown file (e.g., testing.md, api-conventions.md) lives in that directory, can carry YAML frontmatter for path-scoped activation, and is loaded alongside CLAUDE.md. This addresses the team's organization problem without sacrificing functionality.

A.text: Claude Code does not auto-load README.md files in subdirectories as instructions. The documented memory files are CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and .claude/rules/*.md.
A.citation_quote: Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, not `AGENTS.md`.

B.text: There is no .claude/config.yaml that maps file patterns to sections within CLAUDE.md. Path-scoped instructions are configured via paths frontmatter in .claude/rules/ files, not via a config.yaml mapping.

D.text: Nested CLAUDE.md files do not override parents; all discovered files are concatenated into context, and subdirectory files only load when Claude reads files in that subdirectory. They are also tied to directory layout, not to topic.
D.citation_quote: All discovered files are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other.

stem: You want to create a custom /review slash command that runs your team's standard code review checklist. This command should be available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository. Where should you create this command file?

options.A: In the CLAUDE.md file at the project root
options.B: In ~/.claude/commands/ in each developer's home directory
options.C: In a .claude/config.json file with a commands array
options.D: In the .claude/commands/ directory in the project repository

correct_option_text: In the .claude/commands/ directory in the project repository
explanation: Project-scoped slash commands live in the repository's .claude/commands/ directory and are version-controlled alongside the code, so any developer who clones or pulls the repo automatically gets them. User-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are private to one developer's machine and would have to be installed manually by each teammate.

A.text: CLAUDE.md provides project context, not slash command definitions. Slash commands are individual markdown files in .claude/commands/, not entries inside CLAUDE.md.
A.citation_quote: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ (shared via version control) vs user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ (personal)

B.text: ~/.claude/commands/ is the user-scoped, machine-local location. Files there do not travel with the repository, so they would not be available to teammates after a clone or pull.
B.citation_quote: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ (shared via version control) vs user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ (personal)

C.text: Claude Code does not register slash commands via a commands array in a config.json; commands are file-based and live in .claude/commands/.
C.citation_quote: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ (shared via version control) vs user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ (personal)

stem: Your CI pipeline runs the Claude Code CLI (with --print mode) using CLAUDE.md to provide project context for code reviews, and developers generally find the reviews insightful. However, they report that integrating findings into your workflow is difficult-Claude produces narrative paragraphs that must be manually copied into PR comments. Your team wants to automatically post each finding as a separate inline PR comment at the relevant code location, which requires structured data with file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix. What's the most effective approach?

options.A: Use CLI flags --output-format json and --json-schema to enforce structured findings, then parse output to post inline comments via the GitHub API.
options.B: Add a "Review Output Format" section to CLAUDE.md with examples showing structured findings, so Claude learns the expected format from project context.
options.C: Keep the narrative review format but add a summarization step that uses Claude to generate a structured JSON summary of the findings.
options.D: Include explicit formatting instructions in your review prompt requiring each finding to follow a parseable template like [FILE:path] [LINE:n] [SEVERITY:level] ....

correct_option_text: Use CLI flags --output-format json and --json-schema to enforce structured findings, then parse output to post inline comments via the GitHub API.
explanation: Posting inline PR comments needs reliably structured fields (file, line, severity, fix). The CLI provides --output-format json with --json-schema to produce validated structured output in print mode, which downstream code can parse and post via the GitHub API. CLAUDE.md or template instructions provide only probabilistic formatting and won't match the consistency of schema-validated output.

B.text: CLAUDE.md guidance shapes context but cannot guarantee schema compliance; the user already saw inconsistent output from instructions and needs a validated schema instead.
B.citation_quote: Get validated JSON output matching a JSON Schema after agent completes its workflow (print mode only, see [structured outputs])

C.text: Adding a second narrative-to-JSON pass increases cost and latency and still relies on natural-language summarization rather than enforced schema; --json-schema is the supported one-step path.
C.citation_quote: --output-format json and --json-schema CLI flags for enforcing structured output in CI contexts

D.text: A bracket template is still prompt-based formatting; the user already established that detailed instructions produce inconsistent output. The supported deterministic mechanism is --json-schema.
D.citation_quote: Few-shot examples as the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results

stem: Your team has been using Claude Code for several months. Recently, three developers report that Claude correctly follows your "always include comprehensive error handling" guideline, but a fourth developer who just joined reports Claude isn't following this guideline. All four developers are working in the same repository and have the latest code pulled. What's the most likely cause and appropriate fix?

options.A: Claude Code builds per-user preference models over time through repeated interactions. The new developer needs to repeatedly specify the error handling requirement until Claude learns their preferences.
options.B: The new developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md contains conflicting instructions that override the project settings. Have them remove the conflicting section from their user-level configuration.
options.C: The guideline exists in the original developers' ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files (user-level) instead of the project's .claude/CLAUDE.md. Move the instruction to the project-level file so all team members receive it.
options.D: Claude Code caches CLAUDE.md contents after first read. The original developers have cached versions while the new developer loaded after the file was modified. Have all developers clear their Claude Code cache.

correct_option_text: The guideline exists in the original developers' ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files (user-level) instead of the project's .claude/CLAUDE.md. Move the instruction to the project-level file so all team members receive it.
explanation: CLAUDE.md is layered: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is user-only and isn't shared with teammates, while project-level files (.claude/CLAUDE.md or repo-root CLAUDE.md) propagate via version control. A new teammate not seeing the rule is the textbook symptom of a guideline that lives at user level instead of project level. The fix is to move it to the project file.

A.text: Claude Code does not learn long-term per-user preference models from repeated interactions; configuration is loaded explicitly from CLAUDE.md files.

B.text: If conflicting user-level instructions were the cause, the new developer would need to remove them - but the actual fix is to relocate the project-wide rule into the project-level file so all developers receive it.
B.citation_quote: user-level settings apply only to that user-instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ... are not shared with teammates via version control

D.text: Claude Code does not have a persistent "first-read cache" of CLAUDE.md contents that survives across sessions; the file is read at session start.

stem: Your team wants to add a GitHub MCP server to enable PR lookups and CI status checks through Claude Code. Each of the six developers has their own GitHub personal access token. You want consistent tooling across the team without committing credentials to version control. What's the most effective configuration approach?

options.A: Add the server to a project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion (${GITHUB_TOKEN}) for authentication, and document the required environment variable in your project README.
options.B: Create an MCP server wrapper that reads tokens from a .env file and proxies requests to the GitHub API, then add this wrapper to your project .mcp.json.
options.C: Configure the server in project scope with a placeholder token value, then instruct developers to override it in their local scope configuration.
options.D: Have each developer configure the server in user scope with claude mcp add --scope user.

correct_option_text: Add the server to a project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion (${GITHUB_TOKEN}) for authentication, and document the required environment variable in your project README.
explanation: Project-scoped .mcp.json gives every developer the same server definition through the repo, while ${GITHUB_TOKEN} expansion lets each developer supply their own PAT via the environment without committing secrets. Documenting the variable in the README keeps onboarding consistent. This is the documented pattern for shared MCP servers requiring per-user credentials.

B.text: Building a custom proxy wrapper is unnecessary complexity when .mcp.json natively supports environment variable expansion. It also moves credentials into a .env file that must be carefully gitignored without solving any problem the standard pattern doesn't.
B.citation_quote: Configuring shared MCP servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion for authentication tokens

C.text: There is no documented 'local override' scope that supersedes a placeholder in project .mcp.json. Environment variable expansion is the supported and simpler mechanism.
C.citation_quote: Configuring shared MCP servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion for authentication tokens

D.text: Six developers each configuring user-scope independently loses the consistency benefit and breaks for new joiners or CI; project scope plus env var expansion is the documented way to share configuration while keeping tokens private.
D.citation_quote: Configuring shared MCP servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion for authentication tokens

stem: Your CLAUDE.md has grown to over 400 lines containing coding standards, testing conventions, a detailed PR review checklist, deployment workflow instructions, and database migration procedures. You want Claude to always follow the coding standards and testing conventions, but only apply PR review, deployment, and migration guidance when you're actually performing those tasks. What's the most effective restructuring approach?

options.A: Split the CLAUDE.md into files in .claude/rules/ with path-specific glob patterns so each rule loads only for matching file types
options.B: Keep universal standards in CLAUDE.md and create Skills for task-specific workflows (PR reviews, deployments, migrations) with trigger keywords
options.C: Move all guidance into separate Skills files organized by workflow type, keeping only a brief project description in CLAUDE.md
options.D: Keep all content in CLAUDE.md but use @import syntax to organize it into separately maintained files by category

correct_option_text: Keep universal standards in CLAUDE.md and create Skills for task-specific workflows (PR reviews, deployments, migrations) with trigger keywords
explanation: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards (coding standards, test conventions) that apply to every interaction. Skills are designed for on-demand, task-specific workflows triggered by their description - exactly the right vehicle for PR reviews, deployments, and migrations that should activate only when the user is doing those tasks. Splitting along the always-on vs on-demand axis matches the documented trade-off.

A.text: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ key off file globs (e.g. **/*.test.tsx). They cannot represent procedural workflows like 'do a PR review' or 'run a deployment' that aren't tied to editing a particular file type, so they don't fit PR/deploy/migration playbooks.
A.citation_quote: Creating .claude/rules/ files with YAML frontmatter path scoping (e.g., paths: ["terraform/**/*"]) so rules load only when editing matching files

C.text: Moving universal coding/testing standards into Skills means they only load when a Skill is invoked - defeating the goal of having those standards always apply. Universal standards belong in CLAUDE.md.
C.citation_quote: Choosing between skills (on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows) and CLAUDE.md (always-loaded universal standards)

D.text: @import organizes files but every imported section is still always loaded with CLAUDE.md, so Claude continues to see PR/deploy/migration content for every interaction. It does not achieve the 'on-demand only' goal stated in the question.
D.citation_quote: The @import syntax for referencing external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular (e.g., importing specific standards files relevant to each package)

stem: Your team created an /analyze-codebase skill that performs comprehensive code analysis-dependency scanning, test coverage calculation, and code quality metrics. After running this command, team members report that Claude becomes less responsive in the session and loses track of their original task. What's the most effective way to address this while preserving full analysis capability?

options.A: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter to run the analysis in an isolated sub-agent context
options.B: Split the skill into three smaller skills that each generate less output
options.C: Add model: haiku to the frontmatter to use a faster, more efficient model for the analysis
options.D: Add instructions to the skill to compress all outputs into a brief summary before displaying

correct_option_text: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter to run the analysis in an isolated sub-agent context
explanation: The exam guide explicitly recommends using the context: fork frontmatter option for skills that produce verbose output (codebase analysis is the canonical example) so that the analysis runs in an isolated sub-agent context. Only the final summary returns to the main session, which preserves full analysis capability while preventing the verbose intermediate output from polluting the main conversation and crowding out the original task.

B.text: Splitting the skill into three smaller skills still pours all output into the same main session context - the fundamental pollution problem (analysis output crowding the main conversation) is not solved by partitioning the work into separate skill invocations.
B.citation_quote: Using context: fork to isolate skills that produce verbose output (e.g., codebase analysis) or exploratory context (e.g., brainstorming alternatives) from the main session

C.text: model: haiku is not a documented Skill frontmatter field - supported frontmatter options are context, allowed-tools, and argument-hint. Even if it existed, switching models does not address the root cause, which is verbose output polluting the main session context.
C.citation_quote: Skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files that support frontmatter configuration including context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint

D.text: Forcing pre-display compression sacrifices analysis fidelity (the requirement was to preserve full capability) and still consumes the main context with the compression step. context: fork preserves full analysis in an isolated context and only summary returns.
D.citation_quote: The context: fork frontmatter option for running skills in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation

stem: You've found that including 2-3 full exemplar endpoint implementations as context significantly improves consistency when generating new API endpoints. However, this context is only useful for creating new endpoints-not for bug fixes, code reviews, or other API directory work. What's the most efficient configuration approach?

options.A: Create a skill that references the exemplar endpoints and includes pattern-following instructions, invoked on-demand via slash command.
options.B: Reference the exemplar endpoints manually in each generation request by copying relevant code into your prompt.
options.C: Add the exemplar endpoint code with pattern documentation to the project CLAUDE.md file so it's automatically available.
options.D: Configure path-specific rules in .claude/rules/api/ that include the exemplar code and activate when working in the API directory.

correct_option_text: Create a skill that references the exemplar endpoints and includes pattern-following instructions, invoked on-demand via slash command.
explanation: Skills are designed for on-demand invocation tied to specific task workflows (here, generating new endpoints), while CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session as universal standards. Because the exemplar context is only useful for one task type, packaging it as a skill invoked via slash command keeps the context out of unrelated sessions (bug fixes, reviews) and avoids token waste.

B.text: Manual copy-paste each time is the inconsistent baseline skills are meant to replace; the exam guide treats packaging repeatable workflows as a skill as the recommended automation pattern.
B.citation_quote: Skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files that support frontmatter configuration including context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint

C.text: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded universal context; placing endpoint exemplars there would consume tokens in every session, including bug fixes and reviews where they are irrelevant.
C.citation_quote: Choosing between skills (on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows) and CLAUDE.md (always-loaded universal standards)

D.text: Path-specific rules in .claude/rules/ load whenever Claude touches matching files (any API edit), not only when generating new endpoints. That over-triggers and wastes tokens on bug fixes and reviews in the same directory.
D.citation_quote: How path-scoped rules load only when editing matching files, reducing irrelevant context

stem: You're creating a custom /explore-alternatives skill that your team uses to brainstorm and evaluate different implementation approaches before committing to one. However, developers report that after running this skill, Claude's subsequent responses are influenced by the exploration discussion-sometimes referencing abandoned approaches or maintaining exploratory context that confuses actual implementation work. What's the most effective way to configure this skill?

options.A: Split the skill into two separate skills-/explore-start and /explore-end-to demarcate when exploration context should be discarded.
options.B: Create the skill in ~/.claude/skills/ instead of .claude/skills/.
options.C: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter.
options.D: Use the ! prefix in the skill to execute the exploration logic as a bash subprocess.

correct_option_text: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter.
explanation: The skill frontmatter option `context: fork` runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context. The skill's intermediate exploration and discussion stay inside the fork; only the final result returns to the main conversation. This prevents abandoned-approach context from polluting subsequent implementation work, which is exactly the symptom the team is seeing.

A.text: Splitting one skill into start/end commands relies on the user remembering to run the second one and doesn't remove the exploration history from the main context. `context: fork` actually isolates the discussion programmatically.
A.citation_quote: The context: fork frontmatter option for running skills in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation

B.text: User-vs-project skill scope controls who sees the skill, not whether its output pollutes the main conversation. Moving location doesn't isolate the skill's context.
B.citation_quote: The context: fork frontmatter option for running skills in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation

D.text: The `!` prefix invokes a bash command, not a context-isolation mechanism for skill content. Running exploration in a subprocess wouldn't fork the conversation context the way `context: fork` does.
D.citation_quote: The context: fork frontmatter option for running skills in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation

stem: Your team has created a /migration skill that generates database migration files. The skill accepts a migration name via $ARGUMENTS. In production, you're seeing three issues: (1) developers often invoke the skill without arguments, resulting in poorly-named files, (2) the skill sometimes incorporates database schema details from unrelated earlier conversations, and (3) a developer accidentally triggered destructive test cleanup when the skill had broad tool access. Which configuration approach addresses all three issues?

options.A: Split into separate /migration-create and /migration-apply skills, add instructions in each SKILL.md to request a migration name if not provided, and use different allowed-tools scopes for each skill.
options.B: Include validation instructions in the skill's SKILL.md that direct Claude to verify $ARGUMENTS contains a valid name, add prompts to ignore prior conversation context, and list forbidden operations Claude should avoid.
options.C: Use positional parameters $1 and $2 instead of $ARGUMENTS to enforce specific inputs, include explicit schema file references via @ syntax to control context, and add description frontmatter warning about destructive operations.
options.D: Add argument-hint frontmatter to prompt for required parameters, use context: fork to isolate execution, and restrict allowed-tools to file write operations.

correct_option_text: Add argument-hint frontmatter to prompt for required parameters, use context: fork to isolate execution, and restrict allowed-tools to file write operations.
explanation: All three failures map to specific SKILL.md frontmatter knobs the exam guide names: argument-hint prompts the developer for required parameters when invocation lacks them, context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent so prior conversation context can't bleed in, and an allowed-tools allowlist scoped to file writes prevents the destructive cleanup path. One configuration covers all three issues structurally rather than via prompt instructions.

A.text: Splitting into two skills doesn't address argument absence (issue 1) - both new skills can still be invoked with no arguments. Per-skill allowed-tools scoping is partly correct but doesn't isolate context (issue 2).
A.citation_quote: Using argument-hint frontmatter to prompt developers for required parameters when

B.text: All three remedies in this option are prompt-level instructions inside SKILL.md. Prompt instructions are bypassable; the problem requires structural controls (frontmatter fields).
B.citation_quote: Configuring allowed-tools in skill frontmatter to restrict tool access during skill

C.text: Positional parameters $1/$2 and @ file references don't address tool-access restrictions for destructive operations and don't isolate the skill's context. argument-hint and context: fork are the documented mechanisms.
C.citation_quote: Skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files that support frontmatter configuration including context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint

stem: After an initial automated review generates 12 findings, a developer pushes new commits to address the issues. When the review runs again, it produces 8 findings-but developers report that 5 duplicate earlier comments on code that was already fixed in the new commits. What's the most effective way to eliminate this redundant feedback while maintaining thorough analysis?

options.A: Include prior review findings in context, instructing Claude to only report new or still-unaddressed issues.
options.B: Add a post-processing filter that removes findings matching previous file paths and issue descriptions before posting comments.
options.C: Restrict the review scope to only files modified in the most recent push, excluding files from earlier commits.
options.D: Run reviews only on initial PR creation and final pre-merge state, skipping intermediate commits.

correct_option_text: Include prior review findings in context, instructing Claude to only report new or still-unaddressed issues.
explanation: The exam guide's Task 3.6 skill list explicitly recommends including prior review findings in context on re-runs and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. This leverages the model's natural-language reasoning about which earlier findings have been resolved by the new commits, rather than relying on brittle string matching or scope cuts that miss real issues.

B.text: Post-processing string match on file path + description is brittle (small wording changes evade dedup) and doesn't help Claude understand what was fixed. The guide prefers in-context awareness over downstream filters.
B.citation_quote: Including prior review findings in context when re-running reviews after new commits

C.text: Restricting to files in the most recent push misses regressions and cross-file integration issues. The exam guide separates per-file passes from a cross-file integration pass exactly to avoid that gap.
C.citation_quote: Splitting large code reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass to avoid attention dilution

D.text: Skipping intermediate commits sacrifices the iterative feedback loop developers rely on; the documented fix is to keep reviewing every commit but feed prior findings forward to suppress duplicates.
D.citation_quote: instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues to avoid duplicate comments

stem: Your automated code review averages 15 findings per pull request, with developers reporting a 40% false positive rate. The bottleneck is investigation time: developers must click into each finding to read Claude's reasoning before deciding whether to address or dismiss it. Your CLAUDE.md already contains comprehensive rules for acceptable patterns, and stakeholders have rejected any approach that filters findings before developer review. What change would best address the investigation time bottleneck?

options.A: Add a post-processor that analyzes finding patterns and automatically suppresses those matching historical false positive signatures
options.B: Require Claude to include its reasoning and confidence assessment inline with each finding
options.C: Configure Claude to only surface findings it assesses as high confidence, filtering out uncertain flags before developers see them
options.D: Categorize findings as "blocking issues" versus "suggestions" with tiered review requirements

correct_option_text: Require Claude to include its reasoning and confidence assessment inline with each finding
explanation: The bottleneck is investigation time per finding, not finding count, and stakeholders have ruled out pre-filtering. The fix is to surface Claude's reasoning and self-reported confidence inline with each finding so developers can triage in seconds rather than clicking through to read it. Calibrated confidence supports faster routing without removing any findings from the developer's review.

A.citation_quote: Running verification passes where the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding to enable calibrated review routing

stem: Your CI pipeline includes two Claude-powered code review modes: a pre-merge-commit hook that blocks PR merging until complete, and "deep analysis" that runs overnight, polls for batch completion, then posts detailed suggestions to the PR. You want to reduce API costs using the Message Batches API, which offers 50% cost savings but requires polling and may take up to 24 hours to complete. Which mode should use batch processing?

options.A: Both modes
options.B: Neither mode
options.C: Deep analysis only
options.D: Pre-merge-commit hook only

correct_option_text: Deep analysis only
explanation: The Message Batches API trades latency (up to 24 hours) for ~50% cost savings. It fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads like the overnight 'deep analysis' job that already polls for completion. It is inappropriate for the pre-merge-commit hook, which blocks PR merging and requires synchronous, low-latency responses.

A.text: Using batch for both modes would block PR merges for up to 24 hours, which is unacceptable for a pre-merge-commit hook that must complete before allowing the merge.
A.citation_quote: Batch processing is ... inappropriate for blocking workflows (pre-merge checks)

B.text: Skipping batch entirely forfeits the 50% cost savings on the deep-analysis workload, which already tolerates overnight latency and explicitly polls for completion - exactly the profile batch is designed for.
B.citation_quote: Batch processing is appropriate for non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation)

D.text: This is the inverse of correct: pre-merge hooks are blocking and latency-sensitive, the worst fit for batch. Deep analysis is the latency-tolerant workload where batch belongs.
D.citation_quote: Batch processing is ... inappropriate for blocking workflows (pre-merge checks)

stem: Your team uses Claude Code to generate code suggestions, but you notice a pattern: subtle issues-performance optimizations that break edge cases, cleanups that change behavior unexpectedly-only surface when a different team member reviews the PR. Claude's reasoning during generation shows it considered these cases but concluded its approach was correct. Which approach directly addresses the root cause of this self-review limitation?

correct_option_text: Have a second, independent Claude Code instance review the changes without seeing the generator's reasoning.
explanation: Self-review by the same Claude instance inherits the generator's reasoning bias and tends to ratify earlier conclusions. The documented pattern is an independent reviewer instance that does not see the generator's chain of thought, mirroring why a fresh human reviewer catches issues the author missed.

A.text: Better generation context can reduce some errors but doesn't address the self-review blind spot the question describes; the model already considered the cases.
A.citation_quote: Independent review instances (without prior reasoning context) are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking

B.text: Extended thinking is exactly what the failing scenario already used: the model reasoned through the cases and still concluded incorrectly. Independent review is documented as more effective.
B.citation_quote: more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking

D.text: Using the same name in ~/.claude/skills/commit/ creates ambiguity with the project's /commit skill rather than a clean separation; the guide explicitly recommends a different name.

stem: Your codebase has distinct areas with different coding conventions: React components use functional style with hooks, API handlers use async/await with specific error handling, and database models follow a repository pattern. Test files are spread throughout the codebase alongside the code they test (e.g., Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx), and you want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. What's the most maintainable way to ensure Claude automatically applies the correct conventions when generating code?

options.A: Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns to conditionally apply conventions based on file paths
options.B: Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each subdirectory containing that area's specific conventions
options.C: Create skills in .claude/skills/ for each code type that include the relevant conventions in their SKILL.md files
options.D: Consolidate all conventions in the root CLAUDE.md file under headers for each area, relying on Claude to infer which section applies

correct_option_text: Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns to conditionally apply conventions based on file paths
explanation: `.claude/rules/` files with YAML `paths:` frontmatter let conventions match by glob (e.g., `**/*.test.tsx`) regardless of directory location, which is essential for tests scattered next to their source. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files cannot reach files spread across many directories.

B.text: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound and can't reach test files spread across the codebase; path-specific rules are the documented choice when conventions span directories.
B.citation_quote: Choosing path-specific rules over subdirectory CLAUDE.md files when conventions must apply to files spread across the codebase

C.text: Skills are on-demand task-specific workflows that require invocation; CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/` provide always-on standards. Skills are the wrong primitive for automatic convention enforcement.
C.citation_quote: Choosing between skills (on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows) and CLAUDE.md (always-loaded universal standards)

D.text: Relying on Claude to infer which header applies is unreliable; explicit path matching gives deterministic activation, which is the documented advantage.
D.citation_quote: How path-scoped rules load only when editing matching files, reducing irrelevant context and token usage

stem: You've been assigned to restructure the team's monolithic application into microservices. This will involve changes across dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Which approach should you take?

options.A: Use direct execution with comprehensive upfront instructions detailing exactly how each service should be structured.
options.B: Enter plan mode to explore the codebase, understand dependencies, and design an implementation approach before making changes.
options.C: Begin in direct execution mode and only switch to plan mode if you encounter unexpected complexity during implementation.
options.D: Start with direct execution and make changes incrementally, letting the implementation reveal the natural service boundaries.

explanation: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications - exactly the monolith-to-microservices restructuring described. It enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework when dependencies are discovered late.

A.text: Comprehensive upfront instructions assume the design is already known; the scenario explicitly involves architectural decisions about service boundaries, which require exploration first.
A.citation_quote: Plan mode enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework

C.text: Direct execution first risks costly rework once dependencies surface; plan mode is the documented recommendation for architectural decisions and multi-file modifications.
C.citation_quote: Plan mode enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework

D.text: Letting service boundaries 'emerge' from incremental edits invites rework when boundary decisions affect dozens of files; plan mode is selected precisely for this class of architectural task.

stem: You need to add Slack as a new notification channel. The existing codebase has clear, consistent patterns for email, SMS, and push channels. However, the Slack API offers fundamentally different integration approaches-incoming webhooks (simple, one-way only), bot tokens (enables delivery confirmation and programmatic control), or Slack Apps (bidirectional events, requires workspace approval). Your ticket says "add Slack support" without specifying which integration method or whether advanced features like delivery tracking will be needed. How should you approach this task?

options.A: Start direct execution using the bot token approach to enable delivery confirmation capabilities.
options.B: Start direct execution to scaffold the Slack channel class following existing patterns, deferring the integration method decision until later.
options.C: Enter plan mode to explore the integration options and their architectural implications, then present a recommendation before implementing.
options.D: Start direct execution using incoming webhooks to match the existing one-way notification pattern.

correct_option_text: Enter plan mode to explore the integration options and their architectural implications, then present a recommendation before implementing.
explanation: Plan mode is the documented Claude Code workflow for tasks that involve architectural choices or multiple valid approaches. The Slack ticket has three meaningfully different integration paths with different capability and approval implications, so the architect should use plan mode to surface options and tradeoffs before any code is written.

A.text: Picking bot tokens up front pre-commits to one architecture before the team has decided whether delivery confirmation or bidirectional events are even needed. Plan mode is designed exactly for this kind of decision.
A.citation_quote: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications

B.text: Scaffolding before the integration method is chosen wastes work because the three Slack approaches diverge in tokens, payload shape, and lifecycle, not just in a swappable client.
B.citation_quote: Plan mode is designed for ... multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions

stem: You've asked Claude Code to implement a function that transforms API responses into a normalized internal format. After two iterations, the output structure still doesn't match expectations-some fields are nested differently and timestamps aren't formatted correctly. You've been describing the requirements in prose, but Claude seems to interpret them differently each time. What's the most effective approach for the next iteration?

options.A: Ask Claude to explain its current interpretation of the requirements so you can identify where understanding diverges.
options.B: Provide 2-3 concrete input-output examples showing the expected transformation for representative API responses.
options.C: Rewrite your requirements with greater technical precision, specifying exact field mappings, nesting rules, and timestamp format strings.
options.D: Write a JSON schema defining the expected output structure and validate Claude's output against it after each iteration.

correct_option_text: Provide 2-3 concrete input-output examples showing the expected transformation for representative API responses.
explanation: When prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently across iterations, concrete input/output examples are the most effective intervention. Two or three representative pairs anchor field placement, nesting, and exact timestamp formats far better than additional prose, and the model can generalize from them to new shapes. This is the canonical iterative refinement technique for transformation tasks.

A.text: Asking Claude to explain its interpretation can be diagnostic but does not directly correct the output. The exam guide identifies concrete examples, not introspection, as the most effective way to align prose-resistant transformations.
A.citation_quote: Concrete input/output examples as the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently

C.text: Rewriting prose with greater precision is doubling down on the technique that already failed twice. The guide explicitly recommends switching from prose to concrete input/output examples in this scenario.
C.citation_quote: Concrete input/output examples as the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently

D.text: A JSON schema constrains the output shape but does not teach Claude what content belongs where or how to format timestamps. Schema validation catches violations after the fact; examples prevent them.
D.citation_quote: strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors

stem: Your automated code review system shows inconsistent severity ratings-similar issues like null pointer risks receive "critical" severity in some PRs but only "medium" in others. Developer trust is declining because teams can't predict which findings require immediate attention. What's the most effective way to improve severity consistency?

options.A: Modify the prompt to ask Claude to rate severity relative to other issues in the same PR, so the most severe issue is always marked critical and others rated proportionally
options.B: Add a CLAUDE.md file that lists issue types and their default severities, instructing Claude to reference this mapping when assigning ratings
options.C: Include explicit severity criteria in your prompt with concrete code examples for each severity level
options.D: Request that Claude include its reasoning for each severity assignment, then use that reasoning to manually calibrate and adjust ratings during review

correct_option_text: Include explicit severity criteria in your prompt with concrete code examples for each severity level
explanation: Inconsistency in subjective ratings is most reliably reduced by anchoring the prompt with explicit severity criteria and concrete code examples for each level. This grounds the classifier so similar issues map to the same severity across PRs.

A.text: Relative-to-PR severity destroys cross-PR comparability: the same null-pointer issue gets different ratings depending on what else is in the PR, worsening predictability.
A.citation_quote: Defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level to achieve consistent classification

B.text: A CLAUDE.md mapping is not as load-bearing as in-prompt criteria with examples, and it relies on Claude consulting the file. Concrete examples bound to severity levels are the documented remedy.
B.citation_quote: Defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level to achieve consistent classification

D.text: Manual calibration after the fact does not improve the model's first-pass consistency, which is what is undermining developer trust. Up-front criteria fix the root cause.
D.citation_quote: Defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level to achieve consistent classification

stem: Your team has used Claude Code for months. Recently, three developers report Claude follows the guidance "always include comprehensive error handling," but a fourth developer who just joined says Claude does not follow it. All four work in the same repo and have up-to-date code. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.A: The guidance lives in the original developers' user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` files, not in the project `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Move the instruction to the project-level file so all team members receive it.
options.B: Claude Code caches CLAUDE.md after first read; original developers use cached versions. Everyone should clear the Claude Code cache.
options.C: Claude Code learns per-user preferences over time; the new developer must repeat the requirement until Claude "remembers" it.
options.D: The new developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` contains conflicting instructions overriding project settings; they should delete the conflicting section.

correct_option_text: The guidance lives in the original developers' user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` files, not in the project `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Move the instruction to the project-level file so all team members receive it.
explanation: Per the exam guide, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is user-level and is not shared with teammates via version control. Project-level instructions belong in .claude/CLAUDE.md (or root CLAUDE.md), which is checked in and so visible to everyone. Symptom: the new dev doesn't see guidance the original developers wrote into their personal user-level files. Fix: move it to the project-level file.

C.text: Claude Code does not learn per-user preferences by repetition through the chat session. Persistent project guidance must be written into a project-level config; auto memory is per-machine and not shared.
C.citation_quote: Auto memory is machine-local. All worktrees and subdirectories within the same git repository share one auto memory directory. Files are not shared across machines

D.text: The symptom is that the new developer is missing the rule, not that they have an opposing one - the original three see it because of their own local user-level files. There is no evidence of a conflicting override.
