In a monorepo, this lets the root file carry shared rules while each package's CLAUDE.md provides framework-specific guidance, loaded on-demand when Claude reads files in that subtree.

A.text: A single monolithic CLAUDE.md violates the documented size guidance (target under 200 lines) and forces Claude to load all packages' instructions on every session, reducing adherence.
A.citation_quote: Size: target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.

B.text: User-level CLAUDE.md applies only to that user and is not shared via version control, so teammates won't get the project conventions.
B.citation_quote: user-level settings apply only to that user-instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are not shared with teammates via version control

C.text: Path-specific .claude/rules/ are valid for cross-cutting file-type conventions (e.g., all *.test.ts), but a monorepo's package boundaries are directory-based, where subdirectory CLAUDE.md is the more natural fit. Rules can complement but don't replace the hierarchy.
C.citation_quote: Choosing path-specific rules over subdirectory CLAUDE.md files when conventions must apply to files spread across the codebase

stem: A senior engineer adds detailed coding standards and security guidelines to their `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file. When a new team member joins and clones the repository, they report that Claude Code behaves differently and does not appear to follow the team's documented standards. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file is user-scoped and not version-controlled, so teammates do not receive it when they clone the repository.
options.B: CLAUDE.md files must be placed in the `.claude/` subdirectory to be recognized; a root-level `CLAUDE.md` is ignored.
options.C: The new team member's Claude Code version is outdated and does not support shared configuration files.
options.D: The configuration hierarchy requires the project-level file to explicitly import from user-level files using `@import`.

correct_option_text: The `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file is user-scoped and not version-controlled, so teammates do not receive it when they clone the repository.
explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is the user-level scope: it lives in the engineer's home directory, not the repository, so it is not version-controlled and cannot be propagated by `git clone`. Per the exam guide, instructions intended for teammates must live in the project-level CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), which is shared via source control.

B.text: Root-level CLAUDE.md is explicitly a supported project-instructions location. The docs name both ./CLAUDE.md and ./.claude/CLAUDE.md as valid project-scope locations.
B.citation_quote: Project instructions: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md

C.text: There is no documented Claude Code version gate that disables shared configuration files. The actual cause is configuration scope (user vs project), not client version.

D.text: @import is supported but project CLAUDE.md does not need to import user-level files for them to load - user-level CLAUDE.md loads automatically for the user who has it. The hierarchy concatenates user/project/directory files; nothing requires explicit import from project to user level.
D.citation_quote: CLAUDE.md files can import additional files using `@path/to/import` syntax. Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch

stem: A team wants their Claude Code workflow to automatically generate commit messages that follow their conventional commits format (type(scope): description). Which configuration approach enforces this?

options.A: Create a custom slash command /commit that generates a conventional commit message and executes git commit
options.B: Use a PostToolUse hook on the Bash tool that intercepts git commit commands
options.C: Add instructions in CLAUDE.md specifying the conventional commits format and examples of correct commit messages
options.D: Add a Git hook (prepare-commit-msg) that invokes Claude Code to generate the message

correct_option_text: Add instructions in CLAUDE.md specifying the conventional commits format and examples of correct commit messages
explanation: Conventional-commit format is an always-applicable team standard for all commit messages, which matches CLAUDE.md's role as the always-loaded universal standards file. The exam guide contrasts skills (on-demand) with CLAUDE.md (always-loaded universal standards); a format applied to every commit belongs in CLAUDE.md.

A.text: A custom slash command requires the developer to remember to invoke /commit; if they use plain git, the format isn't enforced. The always-loaded universal-standards location is CLAUDE.md.
A.citation_quote: Choosing between skills (on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows) and CLAUDE.md (always-loaded universal standards)

B.text: A PostToolUse hook fires after the bash command has executed, so the commit is already created with whatever message Claude produced. Hook-based intercept of bash output is also more brittle than a CLAUDE.md instruction.
B.citation_quote: Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules

D.text: A prepare-commit-msg git hook that re-invokes Claude Code is heavyweight, adds latency to every commit, and isn't the documented configuration mechanism for team commit conventions. CLAUDE.md is the documented place for always-applicable standards.
D.citation_quote: Documenting testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md to improve test generation quality

stem: An AI engineer is setting up Claude Code for a team of 15 developers. Each developer has different preferences for code style feedback. Some want verbose explanations; others want minimal output. How should this be configured without creating per-developer CLAUDE.md files in the repo?

options.A: Create a CLAUDE.md branch per developer in the git repository
options.B: Each developer configures ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with their personal preferences - these take precedence for user-specific customizations
options.C: Each developer passes --style flags when starting Claude Code
options.D: Use environment variables to control Claude's verbosity per developer

correct_option_text: Each developer configures ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with their personal preferences - these take precedence for user-specific customizations
explanation: Per-developer preferences belong in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is loaded for that user across all projects and is not shared via version control. This separates personal styling from team-shared project rules in the repo CLAUDE.md.

A.text: Per-developer branches are a version-control anti-pattern, not a Claude Code mechanism; user-level memory in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is the documented way to keep preferences off the shared repo.
A.citation_quote: User instructions | ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md | Personal preferences for all projects

C.text: There is no `--style` flag in the CLI reference; verbosity preferences are not exposed as a command-line switch.

D.text: The CLI reference does not document an environment variable for verbosity tuning; user-level CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for personal preferences.

stem: A support agent is configured with get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human tools. The system prompt says 'always verify customer identity before processing any financial transaction.' During testing, the agent processes a refund without calling get_customer in 5% of cases. The team adds 'THIS IS CRITICAL - NEVER skip customer verification' to the prompt, reducing failures to 2%. What does this pattern indicate about the overall design?

options.A: Prompt-based enforcement has a non-zero failure rate for compliance requirements with financial consequences, and programmatic enforcement (hooks) should replace it
options.B: The 2% failure rate is acceptable for most production systems
options.C: The prompt needs even stronger language to achieve 0% failure rate
options.D: The tool execution order should be hardcoded in the system rather than left to the model

correct_option_text: Prompt-based enforcement has a non-zero failure rate for compliance requirements with financial consequences, and programmatic enforcement (hooks) should replace it
explanation: Stronger prompt language reduced but did not eliminate failures, dropping from 5% to 2%. The guide's principle is that prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate when deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations); the design fix is to replace prompt-based enforcement with hooks/programmatic prerequisites that block process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.

B.text: Accepting a 2% failure rate for a financial-verification rule contradicts the guide's explicit position that financial controls require deterministic enforcement, not 'good enough' rates.
B.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

C.text: Even more emphatic prompt language cannot drive failure to 0% - the guide states prompt-only enforcement has a non-zero failure rate by nature. Programmatic enforcement is the documented fix.
C.citation_quote: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate

D.text: Hardcoding the tool execution order in the system removes the agent's judgment for legitimate routing decisions. The documented pattern is a programmatic prerequisite gate (block until prior step completed), not a hardcoded sequence for every interaction.
D.citation_quote: Implementing programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until prerequisite steps have completed (e.g., blocking process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID)

stem: A team is deploying an agent that processes customer orders. The agent must always verify inventory before confirming an order, but occasionally skips this step when the customer seems confident about product availability. Adding emphasis to the system prompt reduced but didn't eliminate the issue. What is the most reliable solution?

options.A: Add even more emphatic system prompt language with all-caps warnings about the verification requirement
options.B: Implement a PreToolUse hook that blocks confirm_order until check_inventory has returned available status in the current session
options.C: Log all orders that skip inventory checks and review them manually
options.D: Create a dedicated verification subagent that runs before the main order agent

correct_option_text: Implement a PreToolUse hook that blocks confirm_order until check_inventory has returned available status in the current session
explanation: The exam guide and the hooks reference both endorse PreToolUse hooks for deterministic prerequisite enforcement. A hook that denies confirm_order until check_inventory has succeeded in the session converts a probabilistic prompt instruction into a hard programmatic gate, which the guide recommends whenever business rules require guaranteed compliance.

A.text: The guide explicitly distinguishes prompt-based emphasis (probabilistic) from programmatic enforcement (deterministic). 'More all-caps warnings' stays in the probabilistic regime that already failed.
A.citation_quote: The distinction between using hooks for deterministic guarantees versus relying on prompt instructions for probabilistic compliance

C.text: Manual review is a detective control after the fact and does not prevent the violating order from being confirmed. The requirement is to never skip the check, not to audit skips.
C.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

D.text: A separate verification subagent still relies on the orchestrator to call it and on the model to honor its results. A PreToolUse hook on confirm_order is enforced by the harness regardless of the model's decisions.
D.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

stem: A developer is trying to debug why their hook script fails silently in Claude Code. The hook is supposed to block dangerous file deletions, but it never triggers. The hook configuration uses 'if' filter matching the Delete tool. After investigation, they discover the tool name in their hook config doesn't match Claude Code's actual tool name. What tool name does Claude Code use for file deletion?

options.A: The FileSystem.delete method - part of Claude Code's filesystem API for file operations
options.B: The Delete tool - Claude Code has a dedicated tool for removing files from the workspace
options.C: The RemoveFile tool - a specialized tool that handles file deletion with confirmation prompts
options.D: The Bash tool with an rm command - file deletion goes through the Bash tool, not a dedicated delete tool

correct_option_text: The Bash tool with an rm command - file deletion goes through the Bash tool, not a dedicated delete tool
explanation: Claude Code does not ship a dedicated Delete or RemoveFile tool. File operations are Read, Write, and Edit, and any actual file removal happens through the Bash tool running rm. A hook that wants to block dangerous deletions must therefore match on the Bash tool and inspect the command, not on a non-existent Delete tool.

A.text: There is no FileSystem.delete method or filesystem API in Claude Code's tool surface. The documented file tools are Read, Write, and Edit; deletion is performed via Bash.
A.citation_quote: Built-in tools - Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob - their purposes and selection criteria

B.text: A standalone Delete tool is not part of the documented built-in toolset (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob). Hook configs targeting 'Delete' will never match.
B.citation_quote: Built-in tools - Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob - their purposes and selection criteria

C.text: RemoveFile is an invented name. The built-in tools are explicitly enumerated and do not include any deletion-specific tool with confirmation prompts.
C.citation_quote: Built-in tools - Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob - their purposes and selection criteria

stem: A team's agent handles multi-step workflows involving file creation, testing, and deployment. They want Claude Code to automatically run their test suite after any file edit, without adding test commands to every prompt. What mechanism achieves this automatic post-edit testing?

options.A: Use the --auto-test flag when starting Claude Code
options.B: Add 'always run tests after editing' to the CLAUDE.md instructions
options.C: Configure a PostToolUse hook on the Edit and Write tools that executes the test suite
options.D: Create a custom slash command that combines edit + test operations

correct_option_text: Configure a PostToolUse hook on the Edit and Write tools that executes the test suite
explanation: Hooks are the supported mechanism for harness-driven automation that runs deterministically around tool calls. A PostToolUse hook on the Edit and Write tools fires after every successful edit and can shell out to run the test suite, with no need for prompt-level reminders.

A.text: There is no --auto-test CLI flag in Claude Code; deterministic post-tool automation is configured via hooks in settings.json.
A.citation_quote: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them

B.text: CLAUDE.md is read by the model as guidance and is probabilistic; the model can forget or skip the instruction. Deterministic enforcement requires a hook.
B.citation_quote: The distinction between using hooks for deterministic guarantees versus relying on prompt instructions for probabilistic compliance

D.text: A custom slash command must be invoked by the user each time and does not automatically run after every Edit/Write; only a hook gives unconditional, harness-enforced execution.
D.citation_quote: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them

stem: A security team is auditing an agent system and discovers that one of the MCP tools makes HTTP requests. They want to restrict which domains the tool can contact. Where should this restriction be enforced?

options.A: In the system prompt by listing allowed domains
options.B: In the tool's description by documenting the allowed domains
options.C: In the API configuration using an mcp_domain_allowlist parameter
options.D: In the MCP server implementation with an allowlist, plus a PreToolUse hook that validates the URL parameter against the allowed domains before execution

correct_option_text: In the MCP server implementation with an allowlist, plus a PreToolUse hook that validates the URL parameter against the allowed domains before execution
explanation: Domain restrictions for an MCP tool require deterministic enforcement, not advisory guidance. Server-side allowlist plus a PreToolUse hook that validates the URL parameter against the allowed domains gives defense-in-depth: the server is authoritative, and the hook blocks even before the tool is invoked, providing guaranteed compliance independent of model behavior.

A.text: System prompt instructions are advisory; the model may comply most of the time but cannot be relied on for security-critical restrictions. Audit-grade compliance requires deterministic enforcement.
A.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

B.text: Tool descriptions inform tool selection; they do not enforce parameter values. A description listing allowed domains does not prevent the model from passing a non-allowlisted URL.
B.citation_quote: Tool descriptions as the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection; minimal descriptions lead to unreliable selection among similar tools

C.text: There is no mcp_domain_allowlist API parameter. The Claude API does not expose domain allowlists for MCP tools as a configuration field; enforcement must live in the server and/or PreToolUse hooks.

stem: A platform engineer is designing an agent that interacts with a third-party API. The API has rate limits of 100 requests per minute. The agent makes rapid tool calls that can exceed this limit. Where should rate limiting be implemented?

options.A: In the MCP server implementation, using a token bucket algorithm that queues requests exceeding the rate limit
options.B: In a PreToolUse hook that adds a delay between tool invocations
options.C: In the system prompt: 'Wait at least 600ms between API calls'
options.D: In Claude's API parameters by setting a request_delay field

correct_option_text: In the MCP server implementation, using a token bucket algorithm that queues requests exceeding the rate limit
explanation: Rate limiting is out of scope for the certification's prompt-side controls; it should be enforced where outbound calls are actually made - inside the MCP server. A token-bucket implementation that queues excess requests respects the third-party API's 100/minute limit deterministically, regardless of how aggressively Claude calls the tool.

B.text: A PreToolUse hook delay is brittle: it relies on a fixed sleep that doesn't adapt to bursts or to the actual token-bucket state at the upstream API. Rate limiting belongs in the server doing the outbound calls.
B.citation_quote: Out-of-Scope Topics: ... Rate limiting, quotas

C.text: Asking the model to wait via prose is unreliable; the model has no clock control and can violate timing instructions under parallel tool calls. Real rate limiting must live in deterministic code at the server.
C.citation_quote: Out-of-Scope Topics: ... Rate limiting, quotas

D.text: There is no documented 'request_delay' API parameter for Claude. Rate limiting must be implemented in the integration layer (e.g., the MCP server), not via a fictional API field.
D.citation_quote: Out-of-Scope Topics: ... Rate limiting, quotas

stem: A developer wants Claude Code to enforce specific import ordering in their TypeScript project. They want: (1) node builtins first, (2) external packages, (3) internal imports, (4) relative imports. Which approach reliably enforces this at the tool level?

options.A: A custom slash command that sorts imports after each edit
options.B: CLAUDE.md instructions describing the import order convention
options.C: PreToolUse hook that inspects the edit content before applying
options.D: A PostToolUse hook on Edit/Write that runs an import-sorting linter and rejects non-compliant edits

correct_option_text: PreToolUse hook that inspects the edit content before applying
explanation: A PreToolUse hook fires before an Edit/Write actually applies, so it can inspect the proposed change against the import-order rules and block or rewrite non-compliant edits at the tool boundary. This enforces the rule deterministically rather than relying on prompt convention or after-the-fact linting.

A.text: Slash commands run only when the developer invokes them, so they don't reliably enforce ordering on every edit. Enforcement must happen at the tool boundary, which is what hooks do.
A.citation_quote: Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules

B.text: CLAUDE.md instructions are guidance the model may or may not follow as context shifts. They don't enforce a rule at the tool layer the way a hook does.
B.citation_quote: Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules

D.text: A PostToolUse hook only sees the file after the edit has been applied. The question asks for tool-level enforcement that prevents non-compliant edits, which is a PreToolUse responsibility.
D.citation_quote: Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules

stem: A developer productivity agent has a `PostToolUse` hook that transforms raw Bash output. Currently the hook appends a formatted summary but also preserves the full raw output in the result passed to the model. Sessions exploring large codebases are hitting context limits faster than expected. What change would most effectively reduce unnecessary context consumption from tool results?

options.A: Switch from `PostToolUse` hooks to pre-processing the Bash commands themselves to produce shorter output.
options.B: Modify the hook to return only the formatted summary to the model, trimming the verbose raw output rather than preserving it alongside the summary.
options.C: Increase the model's `max_tokens` parameter to accommodate the additional context from both raw and formatted output.
options.D: Disable the `PostToolUse` hook entirely and let the model process raw Bash output directly.

correct_option_text: Modify the hook to return only the formatted summary to the model, trimming the verbose raw output rather than preserving it alongside the summary.
explanation: PostToolUse hooks should trim verbose tool outputs to only the relevant fields before they accumulate in context. If the hook returns both the formatted summary AND the raw output, the agent pays for both each turn, which is the source of the faster-than-expected context exhaustion. Returning only the summary applies the documented trimming pattern.

A.text: Pre-shortening Bash commands is brittle and case-by-case; it doesn't generalize across the variety of commands, and PostToolUse hooks already provide a uniform place to trim output.
A.citation_quote: Trimming verbose tool outputs to only relevant fields before they accumulate in context

C.text: max_tokens controls model output length per turn, not how much tool output is preserved in context; raising it does not free context room consumed by accumulated raw Bash logs.

D.text: Disabling the hook leaves raw output in context (still verbose) and discards the formatting that helps the model. The documented fix is to keep the hook but make it return only the trimmed summary.
D.citation_quote: Trimming verbose tool outputs to only relevant fields before they accumulate in context

stem: An architect builds a customer support agent that handles billing inquiries. The agent must NEVER issue refunds over $500 without human approval. They initially put this rule in the system prompt. During load testing, they discover that with extended conversations, compaction sometimes loses this instruction. What is the correct architectural approach?

options.A: Add the rule to custom compaction instructions to ensure it persists through summarization
options.B: Repeat the refund limit instruction every 10 messages to ensure it survives compaction
options.C: Implement the $500 limit as a PreToolUse hook that programmatically blocks the refund tool when the amount exceeds $500, rather than relying on prompt-based instructions
options.D: Use a lower max_tokens to prevent conversations from getting long enough to trigger compaction

correct_option_text: Implement the $500 limit as a PreToolUse hook that programmatically blocks the refund tool when the amount exceeds $500, rather than relying on prompt-based instructions
explanation: A PreToolUse hook that programmatically blocks the refund tool when amount > $500 provides deterministic enforcement that survives compaction, summarization, and any prompt drift. The exam guide explicitly recommends hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance and uses the $500 refund cap as the canonical example.

A.text: Custom compaction instructions still rely on the model preserving and following an instruction across summarization - probabilistic, not deterministic. The guide says deterministic compliance requires hooks, not prompt-side persistence.
A.citation_quote: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate

B.text: Repeating instructions inflates tokens, doesn't survive compaction reliably, and is still probabilistic enforcement. The documented pattern for hard money limits is a hook.
B.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

D.text: Capping max_tokens reduces output length per turn but doesn't shorten cumulative conversation length; long sessions still trigger compaction. Worse, it limits the agent's normal responses for unrelated reasons.
D.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

stem: A team builds a customer service agent that handles refund requests. When a refund is approved, the agent calls the refund_payment tool. They want to add an approval workflow where refunds over $100 require manager approval. The current architecture uses direct tool calls. What is the recommended implementation?

options.A: Add a system prompt instruction: 'For refunds over $100, ask the customer to contact a manager'
options.B: Implement a PreToolUse hook on the refund_payment tool that checks the amount parameter and blocks execution if over $100, returning a message that manager approval is required
options.C: Create a separate manager_approve tool that must be called before refund_payment
options.D: Set a $100 limit in the refund_payment tool's parameter validation schema

correct_option_text: Implement a PreToolUse hook on the refund_payment tool that checks the amount parameter and blocks execution if over $100, returning a message that manager approval is required
explanation: A PreToolUse hook on refund_payment is the recommended pattern: it intercepts the tool call before it executes, inspects the amount parameter, and blocks (or redirects to manager approval) when above the policy threshold. Hooks deliver deterministic compliance, which prompt instructions cannot guarantee for financial actions.

A.text: Prompt-based 'tell the customer to contact a manager' is probabilistic compliance with a non-zero failure rate, which is the exact pattern the guide says to replace with hooks for financial controls.
A.citation_quote: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate

C.text: Adding a 'manager_approve' tool that the agent must call first relies on the model choosing to call it; the agent can still skip it. Hook-based interception enforces the rule without trusting model behavior.
C.citation_quote: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance

D.text: A schema 'limit' that hard-fails amounts over $100 prevents legitimate manager-approved larger refunds from running at all. The required behavior is conditional approval, not a hard schema cap.
D.citation_quote: Implementing tool call interception hooks that block policy-violating actions (e.g., refunds exceeding $500) and redirect to alternative workflows (e.g., human escalation)

stem: A platform engineer is building an agent that needs to handle a task involving both code generation and natural language explanation. The user wants the code in a specific file and the explanation in the chat. Using Claude Code, how should this dual-output workflow be structured?

options.A: Generate both outputs in a single prompt and let Claude decide how to format them
options.B: Use a PostToolUse hook to capture the generated code and redirect it to a file
options.C: Create two separate conversations: one for code, one for explanation
options.D: Use Write tool more for the code file and include the explanation in Claude's text response - Claude naturally handles multi-output by combining tool use with text

correct_option_text: Use Write tool more for the code file and include the explanation in Claude's text response - Claude naturally handles multi-output by combining tool use with text
explanation: Claude Code naturally produces multi-modal output by combining tool calls with assistant text in the same turn: invoking the Write tool persists the generated code to a specific file, while the explanation flows through the assistant's regular text response visible in the chat. No special routing or extra conversations are needed.

A.text: Letting Claude decide formatting in a single text blob means both code and explanation end up in chat; the user explicitly wants the code persisted to a file, which requires the Write tool.
A.citation_quote: Read/Write for full file operations; Edit for targeted modifications using unique text matching

B.text: PostToolUse hooks transform tool results, not assistant text. They are the wrong primitive for routing chat output to a file; the Write tool already writes files directly.
B.citation_quote: Read/Write for full file operations; Edit for targeted modifications using unique text matching

C.text: Splitting into two conversations destroys context sharing between code and explanation, doubles the token cost, and is unnecessary because a single turn can both call Write and emit chat text.
C.citation_quote: Read/Write for full file operations; Edit for targeted modifications using unique text matching

stem: A team is adding a caching layer to an existing microservice. The service was written two years ago by engineers who are no longer on the team, and its internal patterns for dependency injection and lifecycle management are unfamiliar to the current developer. Before writing any code, the developer wants to ensure Claude surfaces all relevant design considerations. Which iterative refinement technique is most appropriate?

options.A: Start with a minimal proof-of-concept cache for one endpoint and iterate by describing any failures encountered during testing.
options.B: Ask Claude to implement a generic Redis-based caching layer using standard patterns for the framework, then review its output for compatibility issues.
options.C: Use the interview pattern: ask Claude to question you about the service's architecture, existing lifecycle hooks, and caching requirements before proposing any design.
options.D: Provide the service's entry point files to Claude and ask it to generate a caching design document for review.

correct_option_text: Use the interview pattern: ask Claude to question you about the service's architecture, existing lifecycle hooks, and caching requirements before proposing any design.
explanation: The interview pattern asks Claude to question the developer about the unfamiliar service before proposing a design. This surfaces hidden constraints (lifecycle hooks, DI conventions, invalidation strategies, failure modes) that the developer may not anticipate, avoiding wasted iteration on a generic design that doesn't fit the legacy patterns.

A.text: Iterate-from-failure is reactive; it discovers constraints only after wasted effort and may never expose foundational issues like incompatible lifecycle hooks.
A.citation_quote: Using the interview pattern to surface design considerations (e.g., cache invalidation strategies, failure modes) before implementing solutions in unfamiliar domains

B.text: Asking for a generic Redis design ignores the unfamiliar internal patterns and produces something that may conflict with the existing DI/lifecycle conventions.
B.citation_quote: Using the interview pattern to surface design considerations (e.g., cache invalidation strategies, failure modes) before implementing solutions in unfamiliar domains

D.text: Feeding entry points and asking for a doc skips the bidirectional probing that surfaces non-obvious considerations; it produces a one-shot proposal rather than a collaborative exploration.
D.citation_quote: Using the interview pattern to surface design considerations (e.g., cache invalidation strategies, failure modes) before implementing solutions in unfamiliar domains

stem: A team is implementing a multi-step workflow where Claude first plans, then executes. They use the plan mode in Claude Code (Shift+Tab) for the planning phase. During planning, Claude suggests a risky database migration that the developer wants to modify before execution. What is the correct workflow?

options.A: Edit Claude's plan text directly in the chat and re-submit
options.B: Accept the plan and use hooks to prevent the risky migration during execution
options.C: Cancel the plan and start a new conversation with more specific instructions
options.D: Review the plan, provide feedback in plan mode iterations until the plan is satisfactory, then switch to execution mode where Claude implements the refined plan

correct_option_text: Review the plan, provide feedback in plan mode iterations until the plan is satisfactory, then switch to execution mode where Claude implements the refined plan
explanation: Plan mode is iterative: the developer reviews each plan, gives feedback, and lets Claude refine until the plan is acceptable. Only then do they exit plan mode for execution. This loop is the documented pattern for combining safe planning with controlled implementation.

A.text: Plan mode is not a free-text editor - the developer iterates by giving feedback to Claude, who refines the plan. Direct text editing is not the documented workflow.
A.citation_quote: Combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation

B.text: Hooks can guard against specific commands at execution, but the right time to fix a bad plan is during planning iteration, not by accepting a known-risky plan and hoping a hook intercepts it.
B.citation_quote: Plan mode enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework

C.text: Discarding the conversation loses the context Claude has already built. Plan mode is meant to be iterated within the same session until the plan is right.
C.citation_quote: Combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation

stem: Your team has written a bash script that invokes Claude Code as part of a CI pipeline step. When the script runs in your automated environment, the job hangs indefinitely after the Claude Code process starts and never produces output. Local runs complete successfully. What is the most likely cause, and what is the correct fix?

options.A: The CLAUDE.md file is not found in the CI environment; add a step to copy CLAUDE.md to the working directory before the Claude Code invocation.
options.B: Claude Code is waiting for interactive input because it was invoked without the `-p` (or `--print`) flag; add `-p` to run in non-interactive mode.
options.C: The CI environment lacks a display, preventing Claude Code from rendering its terminal UI; set the TERM environment variable to `dumb` to suppress the TUI.
options.D: The API key is not available in CI; the hang is a silent auth failure; add the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to the CI environment secrets.

correct_option_text: Claude Code is waiting for interactive input because it was invoked without the `-p` (or `--print`) flag; add `-p` to run in non-interactive mode.
explanation: The exam guide states: 'The -p (or --print) flag for running Claude Code in non-interactive mode in automated pipelines' and 'Running Claude Code in CI with the -p flag to prevent interactive input hangs.' Without -p, Claude Code expects a human at the terminal and blocks waiting for input — which produces exactly the described behavior: hangs in CI, works locally (where a human is present). The CLAUDE.md issue (A) would produce an error or degraded output, not a hang. A display issue (C) is not the documented cause of CI hangs in Claude Code; the -p flag is. Auth failure (D) typically produces an immediate error, not a silent hang.

A.text: A missing CLAUDE.md file does not cause Claude Code to hang — it either proceeds without project context or raises an error about missing configuration. The symptom (indefinite hang that works locally) is characteristic of a process waiting for terminal input, not a missing file. CLAUDE.md absence would manifest as degraded or error output, not silence.
A.citation_quote: CLAUDE.md as the mechanism for providing project context (testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria) to CI-invoked Claude Code

C.text: Claude Code's CI hang issue is caused by interactive mode, not terminal display rendering. The exam guide documents the -p flag specifically for non-interactive pipeline use, with no mention of TERM variable or display requirements as a remediation path. Setting TERM=dumb is a workaround for TUI display issues in some tools, but it does not address the root cause of interactive mode waiting for input.
C.no_grounding_reason: TERM variable handling is not covered in the exam guide; this is practitioner knowledge that the TERM workaround does not fix interactive-mode hangs.

D.text: An authentication failure typically produces an immediate error message (connection refused, 401 unauthorized) rather than an indefinite hang. More importantly, the question states that local runs work, implying the API key is available in the developer's environment. The hang-in-CI-works-locally pattern combined with no error output is specifically the interactive-mode-waiting-for-input symptom, not an auth failure symptom.
D.no_grounding_reason: Auth failure failure mode (immediate error vs silent hang) is a practitioner observation about API client behavior, not directly cited in the exam guide.

stem: Your team has created a custom `/analyze-codebase` skill that performs deep exploration of large repositories and produces verbose output. After deployment, two problems have emerged: (1) the skill's lengthy output is cluttering the main conversation context, making it hard to continue working after the skill runs; (2) the skill occasionally uses destructive Bash operations like `git reset` because the developer forgot to restrict tool access when authoring the skill file. Where should you make changes to fix both issues?

options.A: Add a PostToolUse hook in settings.json that intercepts the skill's tool calls to filter its output and block destructive Bash commands after the skill completes.
options.B: Add instructions to the skill's prompt body telling Claude to avoid destructive operations and to produce a brief summary instead of the full exploration output.
options.C: In the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter, add `context: fork` to run the skill in an isolated sub-agent context (preventing output from polluting the main session) and `allowed-tools: [Read, Grep, Glob]` to restrict tool access to read-only operations, blocking Bash entirely.
options.D: Move the skill to `~/.claude/skills/` so it runs with the user's personal settings, which have destructive Bash commands disabled by default.

correct_option_text: In the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter, add `context: fork` to run the skill in an isolated sub-agent context (preventing output from polluting the main session) and `allowed-tools: [Read, Grep, Glob]` to restrict tool access to read-only operations, blocking Bash entirely.
explanation: The exam guide covers both frontmatter fields directly: 'Skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files that support frontmatter configuration including context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint.' Context: fork 'running skills in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation' — this directly addresses problem (1). Configuring 'allowed-tools in skill frontmatter to restrict tool access during skill execution (e.g., limiting to file write operations to prevent destructive actions)' — this directly addresses problem (2). Both problems are skill-level configuration concerns, and both have documented frontmatter solutions. Hooks (A, B) are the wrong layer for skill UX and behavior — they intercept at the tool-execution level, not the skill-invocation level, and cannot implement context isolation.

A.text: PostToolUse hooks fire after each tool call completes and can transform results, but they cannot implement context isolation — the skill's verbose output has already entered the main conversation before the hook sees it. Hooks operate at the individual tool-call layer, not at the skill-invocation layer. The context: fork frontmatter field is the documented mechanism for output isolation; there is no hook-based equivalent.
A.citation_quote: Using context: fork to isolate skills that produce verbose output (e.g., codebase analysis) or exploratory context (e.g., brainstorming alternatives) from the main session

B.text: Adding instructions to the skill's prompt body is prompt-level guidance — probabilistic compliance. The exam guide distinguishes between prompt-based behavioral guidance and structural frontmatter configuration. For tool restriction, the documented mechanism is `allowed-tools` in frontmatter (a structural whitelist), not a prompt instruction saying 'avoid destructive operations.' Similarly, asking Claude to summarize rather than produce verbose output via instructions doesn't isolate the output from the main conversation context the way `context: fork` does.
B.citation_quote: Configuring allowed-tools in skill frontmatter to restrict tool access during skill execution (e.g., limiting to file write operations to prevent destructive actions)

D.text: Moving the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ makes it a personal skill available only to the current user and not shared via version control — it does not fix either problem. Personal skills do not inherit any special 'destructive commands disabled' default; they follow the same tool access rules as project skills. The fix for both problems is frontmatter configuration (context: fork + allowed-tools), which applies regardless of where the skill file lives.
D.citation_quote: Personal skill customization: creating personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names to avoid affecting teammates

stem: You ask Claude Code to implement a function that transforms API responses into a normalized internal format. Claude produces an implementation, but when you test it, two of your five test cases fail — one involving null values in nested objects and one involving timestamps in a non-ISO format. You share the failing test output with Claude and ask it to fix the issues. Claude produces a revised implementation that fixes the timestamp case but introduces a new edge case failure in a previously-passing test. Inspection reveals that the null-value case and the regression both involve the same `_normalize_date()` helper, indicating they share a code path. What iterative refinement technique most effectively resolves both issues without regressing passing tests?

options.A: Ask Claude to fix the remaining null-value case and the new regression in a single message, describing both issues together.
options.B: Fix the issues sequentially: first ask Claude to address only the null-value case, verify it passes, then address the regression in a separate follow-up.
options.C: Provide Claude with specific test cases as concrete input/output examples — showing the null input and expected normalized output, and the regression test's input and expected output — rather than describing both failures in prose.
options.D: Switch to a different approach: write a more comprehensive natural language specification of the transformation rules, then ask Claude to reimplement from scratch.

correct_option_text: Ask Claude to fix the remaining null-value case and the new regression in a single message, describing both issues together.
explanation: The exam guide covers iterative refinement techniques: 'When to provide all issues in a single message (interacting problems) versus fixing them sequentially (independent problems).' The key distinction is whether the issues interact. A null-value case in nested objects and a timestamp regression introduced by the previous fix are likely interacting: the fix that caused the regression may have changed shared logic that also affects null handling. Addressing them in separate sequential messages risks introducing another regression with the first fix, making convergence slower. The exam guide recommends providing all interacting issues in a single message. Option B (sequential) is correct for independent issues; C (concrete examples) improves communication quality but doesn't address the interacting-vs-independent decision; D (reimplement from scratch) is excessive for two edge case failures.

B.text: Sequential fixing is correct when problems are independent — fixing one doesn't affect the other. Here, the regression was introduced by Claude's previous fix, suggesting the null-value handling and the code path affected by the previous fix share implementation logic. Fixing the null-value case first may introduce another regression, requiring more iterations to converge. The exam guide recommends single-message multi-issue reporting specifically for interacting problems — where fixing one affects another.
B.citation_quote: Addressing multiple interacting issues in a single detailed message when fixes interact, versus sequential iteration for independent issues

C.text: Providing concrete input/output examples is an excellent technique for communicating expected behavior — the exam guide recommends '2-3 concrete input/output examples to clarify transformation requirements when natural language descriptions produce inconsistent results.' But option C addresses communication clarity, not the interacting-vs-independent decision. The question is whether to address the null-value case and the regression at once or sequentially; examples help convey the expected behavior but don't resolve the sequencing question. Option A with concrete examples would be the ideal combination.
C.citation_quote: Providing 2-3 concrete input/output examples to clarify transformation requirements when natural language descriptions produce inconsistent results

D.text: Reimplementing from scratch is excessive when the implementation is mostly correct (three of five tests pass) and the remaining failures are edge cases. The exam guide's iterative refinement techniques are designed specifically to drive incremental improvement on near-correct implementations, not to restart from specification. From-scratch reimplementation would also lose the passing behavior already achieved for the three working test cases.
D.no_grounding_reason: Proportionality of response to the number of failing tests is a practitioner judgment; the exam guide covers iterative refinement techniques but doesn't quantify the threshold for reimplementation.

stem: Your team has assigned Claude Code to implement a significant new feature: migrating 45+ files from a legacy date library to a modern one. The migration involves changing import statements, updating function call signatures, and adjusting test fixtures across the codebase. Some files may have library-specific edge cases. Before Claude Code starts making changes, what approach most effectively sets Claude Code up for success on this task?

options.A: Start with direct execution mode and ask Claude Code to make all changes at once, relying on its ability to handle the migration comprehensively in a single pass.
options.B: Provide a detailed step-by-step specification of exactly how each file type should be migrated, including specific grep patterns to find affected code and exact replacement syntax.
options.C: Enter plan mode first so Claude Code can explore the codebase, identify the scope of the migration, understand library-specific edge cases across file types, and propose a migration approach before making any changes.
options.D: Break the migration into 45+ individual tasks, one per file, and ask Claude Code to process each file as a separate session to avoid context window issues.

correct_option_text: Enter plan mode first so Claude Code can explore the codebase, identify the scope of the migration, understand library-specific edge cases across file types, and propose a migration approach before making any changes.
explanation: The exam guide covers plan mode vs direct execution: 'Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications.' It also notes 'Selecting plan mode for tasks with architectural implications (e.g., microservice restructuring, library migrations affecting 45+ files, choosing between integration approaches).' This migration matches the canonical plan-mode use case: multi-file changes, potential edge cases by file type, multiple valid migration approaches. Plan mode enables codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, 'preventing costly rework.' Option A (direct execution) risks incomplete or inconsistent migration across 45+ files without upfront exploration. Option B (providing exhaustive specification) assumes the engineer has already done the exploration that plan mode would do — and may miss edge cases the codebase reveals. Option D (45+ separate sessions) loses cross-file context that's valuable for consistent migration.

A.text: Direct execution on a 45+ file migration without upfront exploration risks inconsistent changes and missed edge cases. The exam guide contrasts 'direct execution for well-understood changes with clear scope (e.g., a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace)' with plan mode for large-scale multi-file changes. A library migration is not a well-understood single-scope change — it requires discovery of how the library is used across different file types before the right migration approach can be determined.
A.citation_quote: Selecting direct execution for well-understood changes with clear scope (e.g., a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, adding a date validation conditional)

B.text: Providing an exhaustive step-by-step specification assumes the engineer has already explored the codebase and identified all file types, edge cases, and grep patterns. If the engineer has done this analysis, plan mode would add little value — but typically the engineer does not have this complete picture upfront, which is exactly why plan mode exists. Exhaustive upfront specification for 45+ files is itself a significant effort, and plan mode accomplishes the same exploration more efficiently.
B.citation_quote: Plan mode enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes, preventing costly rework

D.text: Processing each file in a separate session eliminates the cross-file context that makes a consistent migration possible. A library migration may have interdependencies — type definitions changed in one file that affect how other files should be updated, or helper utilities that should be refactored once rather than duplicated across files. Separate sessions can't reason about these cross-file patterns. The exam guide recommends plan mode for this scenario, not session fragmentation.
D.no_grounding_reason: Cross-file context value in multi-file migrations is a practitioner principle; the exam guide recommends plan mode for the scenario but doesn't contrast it with session-per-file approaches.

stem: Your codebase has both React frontend code and a Python backend. Test files are spread throughout the repository — `*.test.tsx` files are in the `src/` directory alongside components, and `test_*.py` files are in `backend/` subdirectories near the modules they test. You want Claude Code to automatically apply React testing conventions (RTL patterns, mock strategies) when editing `.test.tsx` files and Python testing conventions (pytest fixtures, assertion styles) when editing `test_*.py` files. The conventions should load automatically without Claude Code needing to know which convention applies. What is the most appropriate configuration mechanism?

options.A: Create two separate CLAUDE.md files — one at `src/` level with React conventions and one at `backend/` level with Python conventions, since CLAUDE.md files are directory-scoped.
options.B: Add both React and Python testing conventions to the root CLAUDE.md file so they're always loaded, with a note: 'Apply React conventions to .test.tsx files and Python conventions to test_*.py files.'
options.C: Create two files in `.claude/rules/` — `react-testing.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` and `python-testing.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["**/test_*.py"]` — so each rule file loads only when editing matching files.
options.D: Create two custom slash commands — `/react-test-conventions` and `/python-test-conventions` — that developers invoke manually before editing test files of each type.

correct_option_text: Create two files in `.claude/rules/` — `react-testing.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` and `python-testing.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["**/test_*.py"]` — so each rule file loads only when editing matching files.
explanation: The exam guide covers path-specific rules: '.claude/rules/ files with YAML frontmatter paths fields containing glob patterns for conditional rule activation' and 'How path-scoped rules load only when editing matching files, reducing irrelevant context and token usage.' The key advantage is also explicit: 'Choosing path-specific rules over subdirectory CLAUDE.md files when conventions must apply to files spread across the codebase.' Here, test files of each type are spread throughout the repo — React tests in `src/` and Python tests in `backend/` — making path-specific glob rules the appropriate mechanism. Option A (subdirectory CLAUDE.md) would require React conventions only at `src/` level and Python conventions only at `backend/` level, missing any test files in subdirectories not covered. Option B (always-load both) wastes context tokens by loading irrelevant conventions on every edit. Option D (manual slash commands) requires developer action and relies on remembering to invoke the right command.

A.text: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load for all files edited within that directory and its subdirectories — they are scoped to directory location, not file type. If React test files exist in multiple locations under `src/` (or Python tests in multiple `backend/` subdirectories), a single directory-level CLAUDE.md may cover them, but only if the test files stay within that directory tree. Path-specific rules with glob patterns are more precise: they match by filename pattern regardless of directory location, which is the exam guide's recommended approach for this cross-directory scenario.
A.citation_quote: Choosing path-specific rules over subdirectory CLAUDE.md files when conventions must apply to files spread across the codebase

B.text: Always loading both convention sets in the root CLAUDE.md wastes context tokens — when editing a Python test file, React RTL patterns and mock strategies are irrelevant but still consume context. The exam guide notes that path-scoped rules 'reduce irrelevant context and token usage.' For large teams with comprehensive testing conventions, loading both unconditionally significantly inflates every session's token overhead.
B.citation_quote: How path-scoped rules load only when editing matching files, reducing irrelevant context and token usage

D.text: Manual slash commands require the developer to remember to invoke the right command before editing test files — if they forget, the conventions don't load. The question specifies conventions should load 'automatically without Claude Code needing to know which convention applies.' Automatic path-based loading (C) vs. on-demand manual invocation (D) is the key distinction. Slash commands (and skills) are for on-demand task-specific workflows, not for always-applicable file-type conventions.
D.citation_quote: Choosing between skills (on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows) and CLAUDE.md (always-loaded universal standards)
